title: POC weekly: Stream hedge & seqlen strategy review

transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-03-28 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~48 minutes
- Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Lucas Nguyen (Redwood SE), Diego Marquez (Aurora ML Infra), Priya Singh (Aurora Platform), Erik Wu (Aurora CTO)

Auto-summary: quick review of last week's microburst tests, focus on TTFT for streaming paths, discussion of sequence-length hedging heuristic, kernel switch trade-offs. Decided to run expanded workload and share configs.

Topics: TTFT, streaming handshake, sequence-length distribution, kernel selection, quantization artifacts, fallbacks/hedging.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we have about 45 minutes on the agenda. Quick roll call?
[00:10] Diego: Diego here, ML infra.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, platform eng.
[00:14] Erik: Erik, CTO.
[00:16] Lucas: Lucas from Redwood, SE.
[00:18] Samira: Great. Goal today — walk through the microburst results and then talk hedge strategy for sequence length and kernel switches.
[00:34] Diego: Quick note — we saw weird spikes last week, p99 was up more than we expected when sequence length jumped over 512 tokens.
[00:44] Lucas: Right, and to be clear those were on the streaming path where we keep the socket open. Our hypothesis is the kernel path wasn't switching early enough and the K V cache refill had a bad interaction.
[00:58] Priya: Sorry K V cache? we saw logs that looked like "K V cache miss" — transcripts sometimes show "K V" spelled out.
[01:05] Lucas: Yeah that's the auto transcript style. It's KV cache, key-value cache. We've got two kernel families in the runtime: fast-attn for short seqs and tiled-gemm path for long seqs.
[01:18] Erik: Can you summarize the microburst numbers quickly? median/95/99 for TTFT on streaming vs non-streaming?
[01:26] Samira: I put the short table in the shared notes but quick summary — streaming median TTFT ~72ms, p95 ~190ms, p99 ~360ms for the baseline kernel selection. For batched (non-streaming) median was higher around 120ms but p99 was lower-ish.
[01:48] Diego: That aligns with what we saw. The p99 spike is what concerns our SREs.
[01:55] Lucas: Important nuance — the streaming path has less opportunity to batch, so we rely on early fast-attn kernels; when sequence length grows mid-request we either migrate to tiled-gemm or keep executing slower per-token steps which hurts TTFT.
[02:12] Priya: Is kernel migration costly? we worried about cache warming and stalling the worker.
[02:18] Lucas: It can be. Migration implies recompile/relayout some buffers on some runtimes — on some hardware it's cheap, on others you pay a microburst.
[02:27] Speaker 1: [inaudible]
[02:30] Samira: So what we proposed was a hedging strategy: start requests on the low-latency kernel, monitor early token growth and if predicted final seqlen > threshold then proactively switch or fallback to a different instance with tiled-gemm.
[02:45] Diego: How do you predict final seqlen? we have lots of generative prompts with varying length.
[02:50] Lucas: We use a simple classifier from the prompt and early token patterns — basically a logistic model with features: prompt length, token type (code vs doc), user_history length. We can share the model and it was in the pilot artifacts.
[03:05] Priya: That classifier had some false positives in the test run, switched too often and added overhead.
[03:10] Lucas: Good catch. The tuning knob there is a threshold and a confidence band. We can require >0.8 confidence before switching. Also we can use a per-customer heuristic — e.g., warming window for known heavy users.
[03:24] Erik: What's the plan for fallback capacity? if you move to tiled-gemm and that instance is busy, do you fallback to hosted variants?
[03:31] Samira: We discussed routing policies: prefer local kernel switch, fallback to reserved dedicated pool (if you enable dedicated), else fallback to lower-cost hosted models which are quantized. There's also an option to return partial streaming tokens while background migrates.
[03:50] Diego: The partial tokens option worries compliance since we sometimes expose intermediate outputs.
[03:55] Samira: Noted — that was more for chat UX teams, not for regulated flows. We'll disable for your account unless you opt in.
[04:03] Lucas: Back to metrics — Lucas shares a slide (link in notes) with a per-kernel TTFT curve vs seqlen. Short summary: at seqlen < 256 fast-attn wins; past ~700 tiled path dominates p99. There's a jitter region 256-700 where hedging matters.
[04:22] Priya: Our production 95th seqlen is around 420 tokens so we're right in that jitter band. We'll upload histogram.
[04:31] Diego: The earlier runs used int8 quant on the tiled-gemm path and we saw quality drift. Are we okay with that?
[04:38] Lucas: There is a trade-off — int8 reduces latency on tiled path but sometimes alters token probabilities for narrow distributions. We recommend int8 for fallbacks where latency is the priority and int16 or fp16 for critical accuracy.
[04:52] Erik: Can we do hybrid? int8 for some layers?
[04:55] Lucas: Yes, we have selective quant profiles in Optimize. The runtime can use mixed quant per-layer, but it's more expensive to validate.
[05:03] Diego: The microburst test — what was the request mix? single-token continuations vs long generations?
[05:09] Samira: It was 70% short continuations (<64), 20% mid (64-512), 10% long (>512) to stress the async growth. We'll share the exact trace.
[05:20] Priya: On logs you had numerous "requeue" events when kernel switch happened. Can those be optimized?
[05:27] Lucas: Requeue is the mechanism we use to move work to a different worker; we can reduce requeue frequency by doing predictive routing pre-request instead of mid-request switching. That's the hedging approach.
[05:39] Diego: Another ask — can you log kernel decision reasons for us to correlate? our SRE folks want an audit-friendly explanation.
[05:45] Samira: Yes we can add decision tags to traces: "predicted_long_seq" or "cache_miss_switch". We'll add that to the staging logs.
[05:54] Speaker 2: [crosstalk] I think that's fine
[05:58] Samira: On the experimental side Lucas proposed a two-pronged benchmark next: A) bigger microburst: 1k sample distributed across seqlen bins to get p95/p99 stability, B) kernel-swap stress where we force mid-request growth and watch TTFT and cost delta.
[06:15] Lucas: For A we need customer sample prompts and a trace of their seqlen histogram. For B we can synthesize.
[06:22] Priya: We'll export a week's worth of anonymized traces and dropbox to the shared drive.
[06:28] Diego: For the dedicated pool — we can carve out 2 GPUs for a week for tests but need a runbook.
[06:34] Samira: We'll send a runbook and config. Also note the runtime has a flag to enable "streaming hedging" — it's off by default. We'll enable on your staging once you approve.
[06:47] Erik: Do we need SOC or security checks to turn on staging flags?
[06:51] Samira: No, for staging it's internal, but for production we follow your change control. We'll share SOC2 docs and an IP allowlist.
[06:58] Priya: On observability — can we get token-level timing breakdown? e.g., time in kernel A vs kernel B, network serialization?
[07:05] Lucas: Yes, Console's trace view exposes token timing with a waterfall. We'll show a quick snapshot now. (Lucas shares screen)
[07:18] Samira: Quick demo — here's a trace where the first 8 tokens were on fast-attn, then it hopped to tiled. Notice the stall at hop ~9.
[07:29] Diego: That stall matches our logs. How do we avoid it?
[07:33] Lucas: Two options: predictive routing as we discussed, or keep using fast-attn but increase per-token computation (slower) to handle longer seqs, which degrades median TTFT. It's a trade.
[07:45] Priya: So for us hedging seems preferable to keep medians low while lowering p99 via pre-allocation.
[07:52] Erik: Cost question — does hedging increase cost materially? switching, extra replicas etc.
[07:58] Samira: There's a small cost bump — extra reserved capacity for hedged requests. We estimate 3-7% cost increase for most workloads but reduces p99 by ~30-50% in our tests. We'll quantify on your trace once we run expanded tests.
[08:15] Diego: One more thing — we saw quality regression when tiled path used int8. For clinical text we can't accept that.
[08:22] Lucas: Understood — for regulated outputs we recommend pinned fp16 profiles and avoid quantization. Hedging should route those flows to safe profiles.
[08:33] Priya: Can we add a per-route policy like "no-quant"?
[08:36] Samira: Yes, Redwood supports route-level policy flags. We'll include examples in the runbook.
[08:42] Speaker 3: [inaudible]
[08:45] Samira: Ok timeline and responsibilities recap: Samira shares microburst config; Lucas runs 1k tests; Priya shares histograms; Diego preps dedicated pool.
[08:59] Lucas: Quick technical note — kernel autodetect threshold is tunable by percentile. We recommend starting with 0.8 confidence and seqlen threshold 600 and iterate.
[09:10] Diego: Can we have a dashboard for toggling that knob in staging?
[09:14] Lucas: Yes, we can expose it behind a feature flag. We'll coordinate with your SRE to avoid surprises.
[09:21] Priya: About data retention — if we enable tracing we need to be sure PII is redacted. We'll share our redaction rules.
[09:28] Samira: We'll accept only anonymized traces. Good call.
[09:32] Erik: Any blockers on our side? I think we can do the data export and schedule the deep dive.
[09:38] Diego: We'll try to get things by Friday.
[09:40] Samira: Great. Last Qs?
[09:44] Priya: One small one, you mentioned "staging hedging flag" — what exactly toggles?
[09:49] Lucas: The flag enables predictive routing and kernel decision logging. It also pins fallback quant profiles. Nothing destructive.
[09:57] Samira: Ok we'll enable on your staging upon receipt of the anonymized traces.
[10:02] Erik: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:05] Samira: I'll send a recap and the runbook, and Lucas will kick off the extended microburst run once we have the sample set.
[10:12] Diego: Thanks.
